title: Responding to a $200K–$500K Government RFP in Under an Hour

blocks.text: A take-home exercise for a Forward Deployed Product Manager role at Concourse — an AI-native software company serving government agencies. The task: find a real, open government RFP and build a working product concept using AI tools, with a budget of roughly one hour of hands-on work.

Andy read a live $200K–$500K government RFP, identified the core operational problem, scoped it to a demonstrable prototype, shipped to production, and framed the output as a Concourse product response — not a generic demo.
The RFP

The City of Irving, Texas (Solicitation 147C-26F) was seeking to replace its existing legal case management software with a modern, cloud-enabled platform. The stated scope covered case tracking, document storage, contract and claims management, reporting, and integrations with Microsoft Office 365 and Adobe Acrobat Pro — a full enterprise system replacement valued at $200K–$500K.

items.description: City of Irving, Texas — Office of the City Attorney

items.title: Budget
items.description: $200,000 – $500,000 including licensing, implementation, migration, and training

items.title: Required integrations
items.description: Microsoft Office 365 (Outlook, Calendar) and Adobe Acrobat Pro

blocks.text: Decision One: Scope to the Core Operational Problem

A full RFP response would cover software licensing, data migration, training, and integrations. None of those can be demonstrated in a prototype — and none of them are what a government buyer needs to see to believe a product is worth evaluating. The core problem the City Attorney's office actually faces is operational: tracking dozens of open matters across multiple case types, departments, and deadlines, with financial exposure visible at a glance.

blocks.title: What Was in the RFP vs. What Was Scoped for the Demo
after: Litigation and matters docket with case-type filtering
Deadline urgency indicators and milestone tracking
Financial exposure aggregated by open matter
Navigation stubs showing full system scope

blocks.text: Integrations, migration, and training are real requirements — but they are procurement line items, not demo features. Showing a buyer that you understand how their attorneys actually work is more valuable than claiming you can connect to Outlook.
Decision Two: Name It as a Concourse Product

The exercise asked for a product concept in response to the RFP. A generic prototype responds to that literally. A forward deployed PM responds to it as the vendor: they show the buyer what it would look like to use your product, with your company's name on it, in their context.
The prototype was titled 'Concourse Platform | City of Irving Office of the City Attorney' — not a demo, but a preview of a real product response, scoped to one city and one office.

The application was pre-loaded with realistic Irving-specific cases: vendor contracts under Legal Redline for IT, Police, and Parks departments; civil actions in Discovery for zoning disputes and drainage easements; ordinance enforcement matters at various stages in Municipal Court. The goal was not to show a product could exist — it was to show what using it would actually feel like.
What Was Shipped

items.title: Financial Exposure Dashboard

items.title: Case Type Filtering

items.title: Deadline Urgency Indicators

items.title: Full Navigation Scaffold
items.description: Five sections stubbed: Litigation & Matters Docket, Claims Intake & Triage, Document Ingestion & Triage, Contract Compliance Studio, and Reporting & Analytics.

blocks.text: Technical Execution

Built with Claude Code, deployed to Vercel. The exercise specified approximately one hour of hands-on work; production deployment was listed as a bonus, not a requirement. The prototype was shipped live and accessible at a public URL, which was submitted as part of the application.
Current Evidence
Identified a live $200K–$500K government RFP and scoped it to a demonstrable core.
Built and deployed a working prototype to production within the one-hour time constraint.
Pre-populated with Irving-specific case data covering the actual range of matter types a city attorney manages.
Framed the output as a Concourse product response, not a generic prototype.
What This Exercise Was Evaluating

Concourse stated explicitly that they were not scoring code quality or visual polish — they were evaluating scoping judgment, effective use of AI tools, knowing when to stop, and the ability to communicate a technical output to a non-technical government buyer. The scoping decision (what to build and what to leave out) and the framing decision (whose product is this?) were the actual submission.
